## Response

<!-- RESPONSE-START -->
Cultivation Theory (from Gerbner) argues that people who are heavy and consistent consumers of television will gradually come to see the world in ways that reflect the frequent themes and messages on TV, because those messages are a part of their media "diet." For example, with violence in media: Tv dramas, news, and crime shows often over represent violent events and portray situations to be more dangerous than they actually are in real-life. Cultivation Theory predicts that people who consume more of that content will be more afraid of crime, overestimate the risk of being victimized, or think others are more violent or not as trustworthy. So, before using the Cultivation Theory, I might see "violence in the media" as just a question of whether or not certain shows cause people to act violently or if they are "too graphic," or maybe it is just an issue with the storytelling. When looking at Cultivation theory, it makes me pay attention to cumulative exposure, distortion of reality, and effects of beliefs and attitudes more than behavior. First, with cumulative exposure we don't want to look at just isolated incidents. Instead we should ask the question, "what does watching these films again and again do to someone's sense of safety in the world?" Next is the distortion of reality.This means, what the media disproportionately shows vs what actually happens in the real-world. For example, news broadcasts may show a lot of violent crimes, even if actual crime rates are a lot lower. Cultivation Theory helps notice that discrepancy. Finally, the effects on people's beliefs and attitude more than their behavior is less about someone going out and committing violent acts/crimes, but more about how they view/understand risk, others, and social norms. So, using Cultivation Theory helps me see violence in the media not just as entertainment, but as something that slowly shapes people's worldviews, especially if they are frequent viewers. It brings my attention to the gaps in different people's perceptions, such as what people think is true vs what is actually true, the fear as a public health or social issue, and also to long-term effects rather than just short-term responses. 
<!-- RESPONSE-END -->

## Word Count & Range Check

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
get_response_text <- function() {
  f <- knitr::current_input()
  if (is.null(f) || !file.exists(f)) return("")
  x <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
  # Find the lines that EXACTLY match the start/end markers
  s <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-START -->$", x)
  e <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-END -->$", x)
  if (length(s) != 1 || length(e) != 1 || e <= s) return("")
  paste(x[(s + 1L):(e - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
}
count_words <- function(txt) {
  # Remove code blocks and inline code before counting
  txt <- gsub("```[\\s\\S]*?```", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub("`[^`]*`", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Keep letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes
  txt <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}\\s'-]", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Split by whitespace and count non-empty words
  words <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  length(words)
}
txt <- get_response_text()
n <- count_words(txt)
minw <- as.integer(params$word_min)
maxw <- as.integer(params$word_max)
in_range <- n >= minw && n <= maxw
cat(sprintf("**Word count:** %d  \n", n))
cat(sprintf("**Required range (%s):** %d–%d words  \n",
            toupper(params$course), minw, maxw))
cat(if (in_range) "**Status:** ✅ In range\n" else "**Status:** ❌ Out of range\n")
```
